title: Decoding & Sampling Strategies
summary: How text is actually sampled from a trained LLM, and why that choice matters as much as the model itself.

slides.markdown:
An LLM's final layer only gives you a **probability distribution** over the next token — it never hands you the "answer." **Decoding** is the separate step that turns that distribution into an actual token, and different decoding choices produce wildly different text from the exact same model.

- **Greedy** — always take the single most likely token.
- **Sampling** (temperature, top-k, top-p) — pick randomly, weighted by probability.
- **Beam search** — track several candidate sequences at once.

Same weights, same prompt, different decoding — different output.

slides.subTitle: Always pick the top token
slides.markdown:
**Greedy decoding** picks the single highest-probability token at every step, no randomness at all. It's deterministic and cheap, but it's short-sighted: the locally-best token at step 3 can lock you into a worse sentence overall than a slightly-less-likely token would have.

In practice, greedy decoding tends to produce **repetitive, bland** text — once a phrase becomes locally likely ("I think that"), greedy keeps reselecting it, looping the same clause instead of exploring anywhere else the distribution had real probability mass.

slides.subTitle: Temperature controls randomness
slides.markdown:
**Temperature** rescales the logits before the softmax: dividing by a temperature `< 1` sharpens the distribution (more confident, closer to greedy), `> 1` flattens it (more random, more surprising tokens become viable), and `= 1` leaves the model's raw distribution untouched.

Low temperature (0.1–0.3) suits factual, deterministic-feeling tasks; higher temperature (0.7–1.0) suits creative writing or brainstorming where variety beats precision. Temperature `0` is a special case — it degenerates into greedy decoding.

slides.subTitle: Top-k and top-p (nucleus) sampling
slides.markdown:
Temperature alone still lets the model sample the *entire* vocabulary, including unlikely tokens in the flattened tail. Two fixes truncate the pool first:

- **Top-k** — keep only the `k` highest-probability tokens, renormalize, sample from those.
- **Top-p (nucleus)** — keep the smallest set of tokens whose cumulative probability exceeds `p` (e.g. 0.9) — the pool adapts: narrow when confident, wider when uncertain.

Top-p usually beats a fixed top-k because it responds to how peaked or flat the distribution is at each step.

slides.subTitle: Repetition, frequency, and presence penalties
slides.markdown:
Even with good sampling, LLMs repeat a phrase because each repeat raises that phrase's own probability further. Three knobs push back:

- **Repetition penalty** — flatly discourages any token already generated.
- **Frequency penalty** — discourages tokens proportional to how *many times* they've appeared.
- **Presence penalty** — discourages any token that's appeared *at all*, nudging toward new topics, not just new words.

Tune gently — too aggressive, and the model avoids a necessary repeated word (like a variable name).

slides.subTitle: Tracking multiple candidate sequences
slides.markdown:
**Beam search** keeps the top `b` partial sequences ("beams") at every step instead of committing to one token, expanding each and keeping only the best `b` overall — trading compute for a better shot at the globally-best sequence than greedy's one-token-at-a-time commitment.

It shines on tasks with one broadly "correct" answer, like translation. For open-ended generation (chat, stories) it tends to produce safe, generic, repetitive text — because the highest joint-probability sequence is usually the blandest one — so sampling methods have mostly replaced it there.

slides.subTitle: Matching decoding to the task
slides.markdown:
| Task | Good default | Why |
|---|---|---|
| Factual Q&A, code | Low temperature (0–0.3), or greedy | Want the single most defensible answer |
| Creative writing, brainstorming | Higher temperature (0.7–1.0) + top-p | Variety is the point |
| Translation, fixed-answer tasks | Beam search | One broadly "correct" sequence exists |
| Chat assistants | Moderate temperature + top-p, mild penalties | Balance coherence with avoiding repetition |

**How to decide:** ask whether there's one right answer (favor low randomness / beam search) or many acceptable ones (favor sampling).
